raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|weakener|6858|wealth}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Fastings and mortifications, . . . rightly managed, are huge helps to piety, [and] great ''weakners'' of sin.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, VI. 11.}}}}

'''weak-eyed''' (wēk′īd), ''a.'' Having weak eyes or weak sight.   ''Collins.''

'''weakfish''' (wēk′fish), ''n.'' A sciænoid fish of the genus ''Cynoscion'' (formerly ''Otolithus''), as the squeteague: so called because it has a tender mouth, and cannot pull hard when hooked. {{smaller|The common weakfish or squeteague is ''C. regalis'' (see cut under ''Cynoscion''); the white weakfish, ''C. nothus''; the spotted weakfish, ''C. nebulosus.'' All three are excellent food-fishes; they inhabit the Atlantic coast of the United States, and in southerly regions are misnamed ''trout'' or ''sea-trout.''}}

'''weak-handed''' (wēk′han″ded), ''a.'' Having weak hands; hence, powerless; dispirited.
{{smaller block|I will come upon him while he is weary and ''weak handed.''
{{right|2 Sam. xvii. 2.}}}}

'''weak-headed''' (wēk′hed″ed), ''a.'' Having a weak head or intellect.

'''weak-hearted''' (wēk′här″ted), ''a.'' Having little courage; dispirited.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am able now, methinks,
Out of a fortitude of soul I feel,
To endure more miseries and greater far
Than my ''weak-hearted'' enemies dare offer.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 2. 390.}}}}

'''weak-hinged''' (wēk′hinjd), ''a.'' Ill-balanced; ill-founded. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Not able to produce more accusation
Than your own ''weak-hinged'' fancy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 3. 119.}}}}

'''weak-kneed''' (wēk′nēd), ''a.'' Having weak knees; hence, weak, especially as regards will or determination: as, a ''weak-kneed'' policy or effort.

'''weakling''' (wēk′ling), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ''weak'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' A feeble creature.
{{smaller block|''Weakling'', Warwick takes his gift again.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Henry VI., v. 1. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Jane is not such a ''weakling'' as you would make her,” he would say; “she can bear a mountain blast, or a shower, or a few flakes of snow, as well as any of us.”
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xxxiv.}}}}
'''II.''' ''a.'' Feeble; weak.
{{smaller block|This ''weakling'' cry of children.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXXVI. 570.}}}}

'''weakly''' (wēk′li), ''a.''   [< ME. *''weikly'' (cf. Icel. ''veikligr''), earlier ''woclic'', ''waclic'', weakly, < AS. ''wāclic'', weak, vain, mean, vile, < ''wāc'', weak: see ''weak'' and ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   Weak; feeble; not robust: as, a ''weakly'' woman; a man of ''weakly'' constitution.
{{smaller block|Those that are ''weakly'', as Hypochondriacks and Hysterics.
{{right|''Gideon Harvey'', Vanities of Phil. and Physick (ed. 1702), vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|When I came at the gate that is at the head of the way, the Lord of that place did entertain me freely; neither objected he against my ''weakly'' looks.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}}}

'''weakly''' (wēk′li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wacliche'', ''wocliche'', < AS. ''wāclīce'', weakly, meanly, vilely, < ''wāclic'', weak: see ''weakly''.]   In a weak manner, in any sense of the word ''weak''.
{{smaller block|If a shoemaker should have no shoes in his shop, but only work as he is bespoken, he should be ''weakly'' customed.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii. 219.}}}}

'''weak-minded''' (wēk′mīn″ded), ''a.'' Of a weak mind; of feeble intellect; also, indicating weakness of mind.

{{smaller block|The Duke of York . . . prevailed for a time, and fruitlessly endeavoured to bind a ''weak-minded'' king by pledges.
{{right|''J. Gairdner'', Richard III., i.}}}}
{{smaller block|If he should go abroad, his mother might think he had some ''weak-minded'' view of joining Julia Dallow, and trying, with however little hope, to win her back.
{{right|''H. James'', Tragic Muse, xxxv.}}}}

'''weak-mindedness''' (wēk′mīn″ded-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being weak-minded; irresolution; indecision.

{{smaller block|In homicidal maniacal cases there may be melancholy or ''weak-mindedness'' from the outset and no maniacal excitement. {{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 449.}}}}

'''weakness''' (wēk′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''weikenes'', ''weykenesse''; cf. AS. ''wācnys'', weakness, < ''wāc'', weak: see ''weak'' and ''-ness''.]   The state or character of being weak, in any sense; also, a weak point.

<poem>Syn ''weikenes'' of women may not wele stryve,
Ne haue no might tawardes men maistries to fend.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3325.}}}}
<poem>I think it is the ''weakness'' of mine eyes
That shapes this monstrous apparition.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 3. 276.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Weakness'' is a negative term, and imports the absence of strength. It is, besides, a relative term, and accordingly imports the absence of such a quantity of strength as makes the share possessed by the person in question less than that of some person he is compared to.
{{right|''Bentham'', Introd. to Morals and Legislation, vi. 8, note.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is one of the prime ''weaknesses'' of a democracy to be satisfied with the second-best if it appear to answer the purpose tolerably well, and to be cheaper—as it never is in the long run. {{right|''Lowell'', Harvard Anniversary, 1886.}}}}

'''weak-sighted''' (wēk′sī″ted), ''a.'' Having weak sight.   ''A. Tucker.''

'''weak-spirited''' (wēk′spir″i-ted), ''a.'' Having a weak or timorous spirit; pusillanimous.   ''Scott.''

'''weaky''' (wē′ki), ''a.''   [< ''weak'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Moist; watery. [Prov. Eng.]

'''weal<sup>1</sup>''' (wēl), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wele'', ''weole'', < AS. ''wela'', ''weala'', ''weola'', weal, wealth, prosperity (= OS. ''welo'' = OHG. ''wela'', ''wola'', MHG. ''wole'', G. ''wol'', ''wohl'' = Sw. ''väl'' = Dan. ''vel'', weal, welfare), < ''wel'', well: see ''well''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''wealth''.]   '''1.''' Wealth; riches; hence, prosperity; success; happiness; well-being; the state of being well or prosperous: as, come ''weal'' or woe.
{{smaller block|<poem>Unwise is he that can no ''wele'' endure.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Envoy of Chaucer to Bukton, l. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|And of this ye seide full trewe that moche ''wele'' and moche woo haue we suffred to-geder.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 555.}}}}
{{smaller block|In our olde vulgare, profite is called ''weale''.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I sing the happy Rusticks ''weal'',
Whose handsom house seems as a Common-weal.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Glad I submit, whoe’er, or young or old,
Ought, more conducive to our ''weal'', unfold.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiv. 119.}}}}
'''2†.''' The state: properly in the phrases ''common weal'', ''public weal'', ''general weal'', meaning primarily ‘the common or public welfare,’ but used (the first now as a compound word) to designate the state (in which ''weal'' used alone is an abbreviation of ''commonweal'').
{{smaller block|A ''publike weale'' is a body lyuyng, compacte or made of sondry astates and degrees of men, whiche is disposed by the ordre of equite, and gouerned by the rule and moderation of reason. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 1.}}}}
<poem>The charters that you bear
I’ the body of the ''weal''. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 189.}}</poem>

'''The public, general,''' or '''common weal''', {{smaller|the interest, well-being, or prosperity of the community, state, or society.}}

'''weal<sup>1</sup>†''' (wēl), ''v. t.''   [< ''weal''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   To promote the weal or welfare of. ''Fletcher'' (''and another''), False One, iv. 3.

'''weal<sup>2</sup>''' (wēl), ''n.'' and ''v.'' Same as ''wale''<sup>1</sup>.

'''weal<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' Same as ''weel''<sup>2</sup>.

'''weal<sup>4</sup>''' (wēl), ''v. i.''   [Origin obscure.]   To be in woe or want.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''weal-balanced''', ''a.'' An original misprint, in the following passage, of ''well-balanced'', corrected by some editors, but retained by some, and absurdly explained as “balanced with regard to the common weal or good.”
{{smaller block|<poem>By cold gradation and ''well-balanced'' form
We shall proceed with Angelo.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 3. 104.}}}}

'''Weald''' (wēld), ''n.''   [< late ME. ''weeld'', appar. an irreg. form of ''wild'' (formerly pron. wild), early mod. E. ''wilde'', ''wylde'', found in same sense, confused by later writers with ME. ''wald'', ''wold'', ''wæld'', < AS. ''weald'', a forest: see ''wold''<sup>1</sup>. The proper E. form of AS. ''weald'' is ''wold'' (parallel with ''bold'', ''fold'', ''hold'', ''sold'', ''told'', etc.). The mod. spelling ''weald'' represents the earlier ''weeld'', and has nothing to do with AS. ''weald'', unless it is due to Verstegan, who affected the “restitution” of old forms.]   '''1.''' The name given in England to an oval-shaped area, bounded by a line topographically well marked by an escarpment of the Chalk, which begins at Folkestone Hill, near the Straits of Dover, and passes through the counties of Kent, Surrey, Hants, and Sussex, meeting the sea again at Beachy Head. {{smaller|It embraces the southwestern part of Kent, the southern part of Surrey, the north and northeastern half of Sussex, and a small part of the eastern side of Hampshire. These are the limits of the area now known to geologists as ''the Weald;'' but, according to the English Geological Survey, it is probable that the area anciently designated by that name was somewhat smaller than this, having been bounded by the escarpment of the Lower Greensand, which is approximately concentric with that of the Chalk, but inside and distant from five to ten miles from it. This latter escarpment is, however, in places rather ill-defined, so that there the boundary of the ancient Weald was doubtful. The geology of the Weald is extremely interesting, hence the name has become very familiar. The formations covering the Weald proper are known as the ''Wealden'' (which see). The Weald was originally partly covered with forests and partly destitute of them.}}

{{smaller block|The Historie of this Hogheard, presenteth to my minde an opinion, that some men mainteine touching this ''Weald:'' which is that it was a great while togither in manner nothing els but a desart, and waste Wildernesse, not planted with Townes, or peopled with men, as the outsides of the shyre were, but stored and stuffed with heards of Deere, and droues of Hogs only. Which conceit, though happily it may seem to many but a Paradoxe, yet in mine owne fantaisie, it wanteth not the feete of sound reason to stand upon.
{{right|''Lambarde'', A Perambulation of Kent (1596), p. 211.}}}}

{{smaller block|We know that the ''Weald'' proper, or that part of the country below the Lower Greensand escarpment, was the part latest cultivated. Even as late as Elizabeth’s time swine are said to have run wild here.
{{right|''Topley'', Geol. of the ''Weald'', p. 398.}}}} '''2.''' [''l. c.''] Any open country. [Rare, and mostly in poetry.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But she to Almesbury
Fled all night long by glimmering waste and ''weald.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Guinevere.}}}}

'''Wealden''' (wēl′dn), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Irreg. < ''Weald'' + ''-en''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Weald.

'''II.''' ''n.'' In ''geol.'', the name of a formation extensively developed in the Weald of England (see ''Weald''), and interesting from its position and organic remains. {{smaller|Its geological age is Lower Cretaceous. The deposits of the Wealden, which have a total thickness of 1,800 feet, precisely resemble those of a modern delta, and the organic remains include land-plants, fresh-water shells, and a few estuarine or marine forms, as also dinosaurs, plesiosaurs, and pterodactyls. The Wealden is separated into two divisions: the Weald Clay, at the top, about 1,000 feet thick, and the Hastings Sand group beneath, which is subdivided, in descending order, as follows: Tunbridge Wells Sand, 120 to 180 feet thick; Wadhurst Clay, 120 to 180 feet; and Ashdown Sand, 400 to 500 feet. The Wealden is overlain conformably by the Lower Greensand.}}

'''wealdish†''' (wēl′dish), ''a.''   [< ''Weald'', the Weald, + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Of or belonging to a weald, especially [''cap.''] to the Weald of Kent, Surrey, and Sussex.
{{smaller block|The ''Wealdish'' men. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, Kent, II. 111.}}}}

'''wealful†''' (wēl′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''welful'', ''weoleful''; < ''weal''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''.]   Successful; prosperous; happy; joyous; felicitous.
{{smaller block|For thow ne wost what is the ende of thinges, forthy domesthow that felonos and wykked men ben myhty and ''weleful.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. prose 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To tell the jerkes with joy that joy do bring
Is both a ''wealefull'' and a wofull thing.</poem>
{{right|''Davies'', Holy Roode, p. 13. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''wealfulness†''' (wēl′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''weleful-nesse; < wealful'' + ''-ness.'']   Prosperity; success; happiness.
{{smaller block|In his opinioun of felicite, that I clepe ''welefulnesse.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. prose 3.}}}}

'''weal-public†''' (wēl′pub″lik), ''n.'' The state; the commonwealth; the body politic; the public weal: properly two words, like ''body politic.''
{{smaller block|If you can find in your heart so to appoint and dispose yourself that you may apply your wit and diligence to the profit of the ''weal-public.''
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}}}
{{smaller block|What is all this, either here or there, to the temporal regiment of ''Wealpublick'', whether it be Popular, Princely, or Monarchical? {{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}

'''weals-man†''' (wēlz′man), ''n.''   [< ''weal’s'', poss. of ''weal''<sup>1</sup>, + ''man.'']   A statesman.
{{smaller block|Meeting two such ''wealsmen'' as you are — I cannot call you Lycurguses — if the drink you give me touch my palate adversely, I make a crooked face at it.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 1. 59.}}}}

'''wealth''' (welth), ''n.''   [< ME. ''welthe, weolthe'' = MD. ''welde'', D. ''weelde'' = MLG. ''welde'', LG. ''weelde'' = OHG. ''welida, welitha'', wealth; as ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''-th''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''health, dearth'', etc.]   '''1†.''' Weal; prosperity; well-being; happiness; joy.
{{smaller block|<poem>For I am fallen into helle
From paradys and ''welthe.''</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4137.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I schall go to my fadir that I come froo,
And dwelle with hym wynly in ''welthe'' all-way.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 265.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let no man seek his own, but every man another’s ''wealth'' [but each his neighbour’s good, R. V.]. 1 Cor. x. 24.

Grant her in health and ''wealth'' long to live. {{right|''Book of Common Prayer'' [Eng.], Prayer for the Queen.}}}}

'''2.''' Riches; valuable material possessions; that which serves, or the aggregate of those things which serve, a useful or desired purpose, and cannot be acquired without a sacrifice of labor, capital, or time; especially, large possessions; abundance of worldly estate; affluence; opulence.

{{smaller block|It shall then be given out that I’m a gentlewoman of such a birth, such a ''wealth'', have had such a breeding, and so forth.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 2.}}}}

<poem>Get place and ''wealth'' — if possible, with grace;
If not, by any means, get ''wealth'' and place.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, I. i. 103.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Wealth'', in all commercial states, is found to accumulate.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xix.}}}}

{{smaller block|Things for which nothing could be obtained in exchange, however useful or necessary they may be, are not ''wealth'' in the sense in which the term is used in Political Economy.
{{right|''J. S. Mill'', Pol. Econ., Prelim. Rem.}}}}

{{smaller block|Senior, again, has admirably defined ''wealth'', or objects possessing value, as “those things, and those things only, which are transferable, are limited in supply, and are directly or indirectly productive of pleasure or preventive of pain.”
{{right|''Jevons'', The Theory of Polit. Econ., p. 175.}}}}

'''3.''' Affluence; profusion; abundance.

<poem>Again the feast, the speech, the glee,
The shade of passing thought, the ''wealth''
Of words and wit.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, Conclusion.}}}}

'''Active wealth.''' {{smaller|See ''active capital'', under ''active''.}} ='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|''Affluence, Riches'', etc. See ''opulence''.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
